context: A talk to visitors at a botanic garden

cues.t: Part 2. You will hear a guide giving a talk to visitors at a botanic garden. First you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.
Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

Good morning, everybody, and welcome to Westmere Botanic Garden. My name's Ben, and I'm one of the volunteer guides here. I'd like to give you a bit of background before you go off and explore. The whole garden covers about eight hectares, so you won't manage to see everything in one morning, but most of the highlights are within ten minutes' walk of where we're standing.

People often assume that the garden was created to show off exotic plants brought back from around the world. Those came later. The garden was actually founded in 1672 by the university, to grow medicinal plants for its medical students, who needed to learn to recognise them. Some of the beds near the entrance still contain plants that were used as medicines at that time.

You'll have heard that we've just opened our new Tropical House. It's not the biggest glasshouse in the country; that title belongs to a garden in the south. And although the frame looks old, it's actually new steel. What makes it special is the way it's heated. Instead of burning oil, as the old glasshouse did, it uses heat drawn from deep underground through a series of pipes. That has cut our energy bills by more than half.

Now, a couple of requests. You're very welcome to have a picnic on any of the lawns, and dogs on leads are allowed in the outer garden. But please don't take cuttings from any of the plants. It's surprising how many visitors think a little piece won't matter, but with thousands of people a week, the damage soon adds up.

Our shop by the main gate sells a wide range of plants, all grown here in our own nursery. We used to sell packets of seed collected by our staff as well, but because of new regulations we've had to stop that.

And finally, today's free talk. It was going to be on plants that eat insects, but I'm afraid the speaker is unwell. Instead, our head gardener will be talking about bees, and how we're trying to attract more of them to the garden. That's at three o'clock in the education centre. The talk on composting is next week.
Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.
Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.
Right, let me show you where everything is. If you look at the map, we're standing at the main gate, at the bottom of the map.
The main path runs straight ahead of you, northwards, all the way through the garden. Follow it to the far end and you'll come to the new Tropical House. You really can't miss it.
Just inside the gate, the first path on your left takes you to the herb garden. It's a walled garden in the corner, and it's where those old medicinal plants are.
If you carry on from the herb garden up the west side of the garden, you'll come to the rock garden. It's about halfway up, between the herb garden and the woodland walk.

There are two places to eat. The building you can see just to the right of the main gate used to be our café, but it's now the ticket office and first aid point. The new café is over by the lake, on its northern side, so you can sit on the terrace and look out over the water.

And finally, if you'd like somewhere quiet, try the wildflower meadow. It's right up in the north-west corner of the garden, beyond the woodland walk. It's at its best in early summer, but there's usually something in flower.
Oh, and toilets. There are some next to the ticket office, and another block behind the café, which is usually quieter.
Right. Enjoy your visit, and I'll be at the Tropical House at twelve if you'd like a guided walk.
That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.
